summary: You send a prompt, stare at a blank screen, and then the whole answer drops at once. The AI apps you use every day avoid that by streaming the answer word by word, and you can build the same thing into your own agents. Why AI apps show their answers word by word, and how to build that into your own agents. A language model already generates its answer one token at a time, each token predicted from everything before it. Streaming just sends each token the moment it's generated instead of waiting for the whole response. The model isn't any faster, but time to first token (TTFT) drops, so the app feels much quicker. Under the hood, the connection between your app and the server stays open, and the server pushes each token through it as it's produced, usually over HTTP streaming or Server-Sent Events (SSE). summary: Pasting the same error back and saying "still broken, try again" gives your agent nothing new, so it starts guessing. Give it what you expected, what actually happened, and the full error, and it has somewhere to start. Vibe coding is great until the errors start piling up. You paste the error in, ask for a fix, it doesn't work, you say "try again," and the agent keeps guessing because you haven't given it anything new. Sometimes it rewrites the whole file, sometimes it fixes the original bug and quietly creates a new one. The fix starts with better information. Tell the agent what you expected and what happened instead (you clicked save, the button spun, the request returned a 500, nothing was saved), and include the whole error message and stack trace even if you don't understand every line. For visual bugs, attach a screenshot. Before it changes any code, talk the problem through with it first. Adding "don't change anything yet" keeps an enthusiastic agent from rewriting things while you test one idea at a time. Follow AWS Developers! summary: Automated reasoning uses logic to check whether a precise rule holds for every behaviour covered by a model. This 101-level explainer shows how it can answer questions you could never test exhaustively, and where the proof stops. I use one fictional online shop all the way through: an AI support agent, customer records in Amazon S3, and a database that should never be reachable from the internet. The same question follows each part of the system: what must never happen? A four-line loop shows how automated reasoning differs from testing. Then a real Verus specification shows the harder problem: a formal verification result can be valid even when you asked the checker to prove the wrong rule. From there, I look at how AWS uses automated reasoning in IAM Access Analyzer and VPC Reachability Analyzer. A checker can return a proof, a counterexample, or Unknown. An LLM can help write the rule, but it cannot decide what you meant. The refund example makes that painfully clear: two $300 refunds can slip through a rule that only checks whether each refund exceeds $500. Every result has a boundary. You need to know what property was stated, what was modelled, what was assumed, and what sat outside the model. summary: A founder told his AI coding agent, in all caps, more than once: code freeze, don't touch anything. It deleted the production database anyway. The prompt said no. The credentials said yes. Credentials win. How much AWS access should an AI coding agent like Claude Code, Kiro, or Codex actually get? An agent once deleted a production database after being told not to, because its credentials allowed it. The fix is in the credentials, not the prompt: set up AWS IAM so the agent can do its job and nothing more. Blog with full setup, policies, and commands: https://go.aws/4Ay32QV Follow AWS Developers!
